newsitem.title: USA: Stocks end sharply lower in stormy session.
newsitem.headline: Stocks end sharply lower in stormy session.

text.p: Wall Street ended a stormy session with sharp losses Wednesday after the stock market surrendered a rally after news that the Federal Reserve was keeping interest rates unchanged. Technology shares were big losers.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 86.58 points, or 1.27 percent, at 6,746.90 after losing more than 120 points in a late sell-off.
In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,613 to 908 on heavy volume of 577 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index sank 25.31 points, or 1.84 percent, to 1,348.44.
Concerns that recent strength in the dollar could hurt corporate profits also came into play as investors rushed to take profits on their gains of the past month.

Analysts said the selling first emerged in the technology shares and quickly spilled over into the broader market. Technology shares were key drivers of Wall Street's January rally, which added almost 6 percent to the Dow.
"The momentum players that helped bring the market up are helping to bring it off," said Peter Coolidge, senior equity trader at Brean Murray & Co.
Investors reacted to news that several brokerage houses had downgraded microprocessor heavyweight Intel Corp. and concern about slowing growth at computer networking giant Cisco Systems Inc.
"The market's run out of fuel here to push it higher," said Kenneth Ducey, director of trading at BT Brokerage.
Prior to the selloff, the blue-chip Dow was up more than 40 points as the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee, as expected, kept short-term interest rates unchanged.
Wall Street was also applauding President Clinton's pledge in his State of the Union address to seek a balanced budget.

But analysts said a larger immediate source of worry for the stock market could be the strength in the dollar, which could hurt future corporate revenues at multinational companies. A strong dollar lowers the value in dollar terms of U.S. companies' exports.

"If anything pushed people off the fence, it might be the strength in the dollar," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. The dollar soared to a four-year high against the yen before trimming its gains amid the sell-off in stocks and bonds.
Intel dropped 7-1/2 to 157-1/4 after Prudential Securities and Gruntal & Co. downgraded the stock, both citing its lofty price.
Leading the technology group lower were bellwethers International Business Machines Corp., which lost 4-3/8 to 149-1/4, and Microsoft Corp., off 4-3/4 to 98-3/8.
Cisco Systems sank 4-1/8 to 63. Analysts linked the weakness to cautious comments by Cisco officials about the company's traditionally weak April quarter.

The technology selloff stole the spotlight from Morgan Stanley Group Inc. and Dean Witter Discover & Co., which announced a stock-swap merger creating a financial giant with a combined market capitalisation of $21 billion.
Morgan Stanley shot up 7-7/8 to 65-1/4 and Dean Witter added two to 40-5/8.

"I think there's probably going to be more of those types of deals" in the brokerage industry, said Guy Truicko, equity portfolio manager at Unity Management. The speculation drove up almost all financial industry stocks.
Merrill Lynch & Co. rose 1-1/8 to 86-1/2, Alex. Brown Inc. gained 2-1/8 to 54-5/8 and A.G. Edwards Inc. jumped 1-7/8 to 36-3/8.

Going the opposite way was PaineWebber Group Inc., which fell 2-3/4 to 36-1/8. PaineWebber's stock had surged in recent sessions on speculation that it would be the target of an imminent takeover, possibly by Morgan Stanley.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 10.98 points to 778.28. The American Stock Exchange index fell 3.84 to 585.41.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 4.60 to 408.74. The average share was down 48 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was at 7,498.364, down 94.275 or 1.24 percent.
